r: The applied work is professional-role socialization: orienting an already-licensed RN to baccalaureate-level practice philosophy, nursing theory, regulatory accountability, and professional behavior through assigned readings, reflective writing, and discussion. These tasks map to updating-and-using-relevant-knowledge and interpersonal-communication activities, categories task-exposure research treats as moderately exposed given the course's writing- and knowledge-synthesis load, tempered by the identity-formation and professional-judgment components that research associates with lower exposure. Observed-usage data shows writing and general knowledge tasks are already common AI uses, so students routinely draft reflective essays or summarize regulatory material with assistance. But no accreditor has relaxed the expectation that BSN-completion students complete a formal role-transition course, and internalizing professional accountability is not a task a chatbot performs for the student. Diffusion into nursing-education delivery itself remains uneven. At 24 months the instrumental need to take this course holds.

By 2031, generative tools will draft polished reflection papers and summarize regulatory and theoretical readings with real facility, further eroding the raw writing-execution component of this course. Verification burden stays moderate rather than severe — a supervising faculty member, not a nurse at the bedside, checks the work — so the dampening effect on the rating is limited. What holds the course in place across one catalog cycle is the program-level expectation, common to CCNE-accredited completion tracks, that a professional-transition and role-development course anchor the curriculum; that expectation shifts on an accreditation cycle, not an AI-capability cycle. The rating moves to Medium: execution of the writing and knowledge-summary tasks is substantially automatable, but the requirement that a returning RN actually complete the socialization process is not something capability alone dissolves within five years.

A decade out, AI plausibly handles most of the informational content this course transmits — nursing theory summaries, regulatory explanation, reflective-writing scaffolding — competently and cheaply, consistent with the fast capability trajectory documented in task-time-horizon research. Institutional lock-in is the only thing keeping this from drifting toward High, and over ten years accreditation expectations for how professional-role content is delivered could plausibly loosen or be restructured into shorter, blended formats. The rating stays Medium, reflecting real uncertainty about whether program redesign outpaces or lags capability growth. The honest caveat is that this is one of the more replaceable courses in the track precisely because its core task is knowledge transmission and reflective writing rather than embodied or high-stakes clinical judgment.
NUR 3100.d: This course facilitates transition to the role of the baccalaureate nurse. This course begins the exploration of the nursing program mission and philosophy with an emphasis on nursing theories, evidence-based practice, and regulatory aspects of the profession, professional behavior and individual accountability. This course integrates communication, critical thinking, and cultural humility in the context of baccalaureate nursing practice.

r: The course examines the nursing profession through QSEN competencies, Magnet Forces, and professional-development frameworks, integrating communication, teamwork, and patient-centered care conceptually rather than at the bedside. The knowledge-transmission tasks map to updating-and-using-relevant-knowledge activities that task-exposure research treats as moderately exposed, while the professional-judgment and teamwork-application elements sit closer to the negatively-exposed critical-thinking category. Observed-usage data confirms AI is already heavily used for exactly this kind of framework explanation and written synthesis. The binding constraint at this horizon is structural rather than capability-driven: the course is a stated prerequisite for later required courses in the sequence, so its foundational-scaffolding role caps the rating independent of how automatable its content becomes. At 24 months, capability growth has not touched the sequencing requirement, and the rating stays Low.

By 2031, AI will competently explain QSEN competencies, Magnet framework concepts, and professional-development theory, and could plausibly draft much of the applied-reflection writing this course assigns. Capability trend evidence points to fast, continued growth in this kind of structured-knowledge delivery. Yet the course's foundational role is unchanged: it remains a listed prerequisite for the evidence-based-practice and multicultural-care courses later in the sequence, and a program cannot simply delete a prerequisite because its content is AI-deliverable without redesigning the sequence itself. That redesign has not happened within one catalog cycle. The rating rises only to Medium, reflecting substantial content-level automatability offset by the course's structural position — later required courses still assume a student has completed it, regardless of how the knowledge was acquired.

Ten years out, the professional-framework content is very likely fully AI-deliverable, and the wide-uncertainty capability trajectory makes a stronger claim implausible to rule out. What is far less certain is whether the program will have re-sequenced its prerequisite chain — curricular redesign lags capability by design, and this course anchors at least two other required courses in the track. The rating holds at Medium rather than rising to High: the foundational-scaffolding cap reflects genuine structural inertia, not a claim that the content itself resists automation. If the sequence is ever restructured, this course is a plausible candidate for consolidation into a shorter orientation module, but that is a curricular-design question distinct from the instrumental-need question this rating tracks, and the central case does not assume it happens within the decade.
NUR 3120.d: This course facilitates the transition to the role of the baccalaureate nurse, examining the nursing profession with a focus on nursing theories and philosophy, Quality and Safety Education for Nurses, professional development, and Forces of Magnetism. This course integrates communication, critical thinking, teamwork, and patient-centered care in the context of baccalaureate nursing practice.

r: The course develops the nurse's real-time interpersonal competence in caring for older adults: communication skills for a population with diverse cognitive, sensory, and health status, applied through discussion of cultural, legal, and environmental factors rather than abstract theory alone. Communication skill-building of this kind is embodied and situational — reading nonverbal cues, adjusting pace and tone for hearing or cognitive impairment — which task-exposure research consistently places among the least-automatable activity categories, distinct from the more exposed knowledge-transmission portions of the curriculum. Observed-usage data shows AI's strength concentrated in text and computational work, not live interpersonal calibration with vulnerable patients. The gerontological-competency content is also a standard expectation in accredited BSN curricula. At 24 months the embodied core of the course is untouched, and the rating is Low.

By 2031, AI conversational tools may help students rehearse gerontology-specific communication scripts or summarize aging-related cultural and legal content, but the course's actual product is a student's live, calibrated interpersonal skill with older adults, not a document. The jagged-frontier evidence is instructive here: AI users outside a tool's genuine competence zone perform worse with misplaced confidence, and improvised human communication in the presence of cognitive or sensory impairment sits well outside current or near-term model competence. The gerontological-content expectation embedded in accredited nursing curricula does not relax on a five-year clock, and the older-adult population this course addresses is itself growing, keeping the workforce need in front of any capability shift. The rating stays Low — the knowledge-delivery layer is increasingly assistable, but the interpersonal competence the course exists to build is not substitutable at this horizon.

Even under an aggressive capability trajectory, live interpersonal communication with older adults — reading distress, adapting to sensory or cognitive limitation, building trust across a bedside or home-care interaction — remains outside the class of tasks AI performs on a nurse's behalf; it is a capacity a nurse must personally hold. Ambient documentation or care-planning tools could plausibly absorb more of the surrounding paperwork by 2036, but that changes workflow, not the instrumental need for a student to develop this specific competence. The rating holds at Low with moderate confidence: the wider uncertainty concerns how quickly assistive tools reshape gerontological-care documentation and staffing models, not whether the interpersonal skill itself becomes learnable from a model instead of supervised practice with real patients.
NUR 3150.d: This course emphasizes understanding the impact of individual and societal perceptions of aging and the aging process. Students examine cultural, legal, and environmental factors, and the diverse health status found in the older adult. Communication skills are developed as an essential feature of the care of the older adult in a variety of settings. The core knowledge concepts and role development of the professional nurse in caring for older adults are explored.

r: The course is fully didactic: ethical theories, principles, and decision-making models applied to case-based dilemmas encountered in professional nursing practice, discussed and written about rather than enacted at the bedside. This maps to making-decisions-and-evaluating-information activities, and task-exposure research is explicit that critical-thinking-heavy tasks are negatively associated with AI exposure even as writing tasks in the same course are positively associated — a split that runs through most of this course's assignments. Observed-usage data shows AI is already used heavily for exactly the writing-support half of that split. GDPval's finding that top models approach but do not match expert human performance on real deliverables reinforces that ethical case analysis retains a human-judgment core. At 24 months the rating is Low, driven by the judgment component more than the writing component.

By 2031, AI will draft competent-looking ethical case analyses referencing codes of ethics and named ethical frameworks, and students will lean on it for structuring arguments and surveying positions. The verification burden is moderate rather than severe in this academic setting — a course instructor evaluates the reasoning, not a patient's safety in real time — so the dampening protection is limited. Nursing-ethics content remains a standard, examinable domain within accredited BSN curricula, and no near-term structural change removes it from the sequence. The rating rises to Medium: the mechanical production of ethical-analysis writing becomes substantially assistable, while genuinely original application of principle to a novel, ambiguous case remains a task GDPval-style evidence suggests AI approaches but does not yet reliably match.

A decade out, AI ethical-reasoning assistance will likely be sophisticated enough that distinguishing AI-generated from student-generated case analysis becomes difficult on the page, and the capability trend evidence supports continued fast improvement in this kind of structured-reasoning task. Institutional content requirements for ethics within nursing curricula are durable but not immovable over ten years; accreditors periodically revise professionalism-domain expectations. The rating holds at Medium rather than rising further, reflecting genuine uncertainty about whether the course's assessment methods adapt to AI-saturated writing before its content mandate changes. The applied ethical-judgment core — weighing competing values under real clinical uncertainty, with a patient's welfare at stake — is the piece least likely to be fully displaced even in an aggressive capability scenario, which is why the rating does not advance to High.
NUR 3160.d: The course prepares the professional nursing student to analyze ethical issues that emerge in the practice of nursing. The Magnet/Pathway's to Excellence concept of Exemplary Practice and the QSEN competencies of Patient-Centered Care, Teamwork and Collaboration, and Evidence-Based Practice are explored as they relate to ethics and professional nursing. This course introduces the student to ethical theories and principles as well as ethical decision- making models applied to professional nursing. Students apply critical thinking concepts to applicable codes of ethics, ethical theories, principles, and rules in discussing the ethical dilemmas encountered in professional practice. Values and beliefs are examined in the context of ethical issues, role development, and application in health care.

r: The course builds a nurse's capacity to communicate with dying patients and grieving families under real emotional and cultural weight, examining legal and ethical dimensions of end-of-life care alongside the interpersonal skill development the description names as its essential feature. This is embodied, real-time, high-stakes interpersonal work — precisely the category task-exposure research places at the low end of exposure, in contrast to more textual knowledge-transfer coursework elsewhere in the curriculum. Verification burden is real: a poorly handled end-of-life conversation causes lasting harm to a family and is not easily corrected after the fact, which is the kind of non-obvious-failure, high-error-cost situation that keeps a knowledgeable human load-bearing. AI can summarize palliative-care frameworks, but it does not sit with a dying patient's family. At 24 months the rating is Low.

AI documentation and decision-support tools will be more embedded in palliative and end-of-life workflows by 2031, potentially drafting care-plan language or summarizing family-meeting notes. That assists the surrounding paperwork; it does not perform the conversation itself. The jagged-frontier evidence is directly relevant — AI users operating outside a genuine competence zone, and emotionally loaded, ambiguous human communication is well outside it, show degraded performance with misplaced confidence, which is a dangerous combination in end-of-life contexts specifically. Institutional expectations for end-of-life and palliative content in BSN curricula persist on an accreditation-cycle timescale, not a capability-cycle one. The rating stays Low: the instrumental need for a student to personally develop this interpersonal competence is essentially unchanged at the five-year horizon, even as adjacent charting tasks become more automated.

Even under a central-case aggressive-capability scenario for 2036, the specific competence this course builds — communicating with dying patients and their families in real time, calibrated to individual grief and cultural context — sits at the intersection of embodiment and irreducible verification burden, the two most protective factors in this framework. Ambient and assistive tools will likely handle more of the surrounding documentation and care coordination, but that is adjacent to, not a substitute for, the interpersonal act itself. The genuine uncertainty concerns how AI reshapes palliative-care logistics and family communication support tools, not whether a nursing student still needs to personally acquire this skill through supervised practice. The rating holds Low with the standard long-horizon hedge attached to any ten-year projection.
NUR 3300.d: This course emphasizes the understanding of the impact of individual and societal perceptions of death and dying. Students examine cultural, ethical, and legal factors concerning end of life care. Communication skills are developed as an essential feature of care in a variety of settings. The core knowledge concepts and role development of the professional nurse in caring for dying patients are explored.

r: The applied tasks are literature search, critique of published research, and communication of findings using academic databases in support of evidence-based practice. These map closely to getting-information and analyzing-data activities, a combination task-exposure research and observed-usage data both flag as strongly exposed: literature retrieval and synthesis are core current AI use cases, and the enterprise API data shows a high automation share for this kind of analytical work specifically. Against that, applying appraised evidence correctly to real practice questions carries a genuine verification burden — a wrong evidentiary conclusion propagates into care decisions — which caps the near-term rating. This is not a course whose institutional mandate is course-specific in this RN-to-BSN track, but EBP-research content remains a standard curricular expectation. At 24 months the rating is Low, reflecting execution automatability tempered by that dampener.

By 2031, AI literature search, critical appraisal, and synthesis will be substantially more capable and widely used, consistent with the fast capability-doubling trend documented in task-time-horizon research; the raw execution tasks this course teaches are increasingly something a model performs competently. The verification-burden dampener weakens somewhat as tools mature and appraisal quality becomes easier to spot-check, though it does not disappear — misapplied evidence in a care-management decision still carries real cost. The program-level expectation that BSN-completion students demonstrate EBP-research competence persists, but it is not tied to clinical clock hours the way pre-licensure curricula are, so the institutional cap loosens rather than holding firm. The rating rises to Medium: automatable execution now dominates, restrained mainly by the residual expectation that the course remain in the sequence.

A decade out, AI-driven literature synthesis and evidence appraisal will likely be at or near expert level for routine questions, and the instrumental case for a human executing these specific tasks weakens substantially. The institutional constraint here is the weaker of the two locks in this framework — a program-level curricular expectation rather than a licensure-clinical-hours mandate — so it is plausible, though not certain, that accreditors or the program itself revise how EBP competency is assessed within the decade. The rating holds at Medium rather than advancing to High because judgment about which evidence generalizes to a specific patient population remains a residual human-verification task even as the mechanical appraisal work is fully automated, and this is a genuinely wide-uncertainty horizon for how curricula reshape around that shift.
NUR 3400.d: Students in this course are introduced to the Evidence- Based Practice (EBP) research process. The knowledge and competence needed to critique published research are explored. Students learn how to use research in support of their EBP. Course content aligns with the Magnet/Pathway to Excellence concepts including Empirical Outcomes, Exemplary Professional Practice, New Knowledge, Innovations, and Improvements, and QSEN Competencies of EBP and Patient-Centered Care. Ethical and legal considerations are also discussed. Qualitative and quantitative research processes are examined. Students complete a literature search using appropriate databases on a researchable problem and communicate findings. Emphasis is placed on the improvement of nursing practice through reading, using, and participating in research.

r: The course develops hands-on physical-examination competence: taking a complete health history and performing and demonstrating a physical examination across the lifespan, with graded skill check-offs on interviewing and exam technique. This is psychomotor, embodied work — palpation, auscultation, inspection, and the physical choreography of a head-to-toe exam — which task-exposure research places firmly in the low-exposure, manual-execution category, distinct from documentation-adjacent tasks elsewhere in the curriculum. A missed finding on physical exam is a non-obvious failure with real patient-safety consequences, which keeps verification burden high and protective. AI diagnostic-support tools already assist with symptom triage, but none of them can palpate an abdomen or auscultate a heart on a student's behalf. At 24 months this is among the most protected courses in the track, and the rating is Low.

AI-assisted diagnostic reasoning and documentation tools will be more common in clinical practice by 2031, and could plausibly help a nurse interpret findings once they are gathered. But gathering the findings — the actual physical examination — remains an embodied psychomotor act a model does not perform, and the jagged-frontier evidence is a caution here too: over-reliance on AI interpretation without personally verified physical findings is exactly the outside-the-frontier scenario associated with degraded, overconfident performance. Simulation and haptic technology may supplement skills training, but that changes how the skill is practiced, not whether the student must personally acquire it through repeated demonstration. The rating stays Low: the course's core competence is essentially insulated from the AI-capability trajectory at this horizon.

Even under a wide-uncertainty, aggressive-capability central case for 2036, physical examination remains a hands-on human competence — robotic or ambient sensing may eventually augment some vital-sign or imaging-adjacent data collection, but full substitution for a trained clinician's physical assessment is a much larger and less certain leap than document-based automation. The program's expectation that BSN-completion students demonstrate this competence is not a formal licensure-clock-hours mandate in this particular track, but the embodiment protection stands largely independent of that institutional question and does not depend on it holding. The rating holds Low with high confidence; the genuine uncertainty is about what ancillary sensing tools nurses use alongside the exam, not about whether the exam itself is still something a student must personally learn to perform.
NUR 3700.d: This course is designed for students to develop, practice, and demonstrate their health assessment competence. Utilizing the nursing process, the student collects and organizes data to obtain a complete health history and perform a physical examination. Students have an opportunity to practice interviewing skills and physical examination techniques. Emphasis is placed on the use of critical thinking, health promotion, and demonstration of a physical examination while caring for individuals throughout their lifespan.

r: This is explicitly a theory course, integrating pathophysiology, pharmacology, and physical-assessment findings conceptually to teach the baccalaureate nurse's care-coordination role across acute and chronic disease management, genomics, pain management, and palliative care. The applied task is synthesizing multiple knowledge domains into a coordinated, safe care plan — closer to analyzing-information and decision-making activities than to hands-on execution, and only moderately exposed under task-exposure research given the clinical-judgment component. Verification burden is real and protective: a flawed care-coordination plan touching pharmacology and comorbidity management has direct patient-safety consequences, a non-obvious-failure situation research treats as raising the bar for human oversight. Observed-usage data shows AI already assists with drafting care-plan documentation, but assembling a safe, individualized coordination plan under this dampener keeps the rating Low at 24 months.

By 2031, AI decision-support tools will likely draft more complete care-coordination plans, flag drug interactions, and summarize disease-management guidelines with real competence, consistent with the fast capability trajectory in this kind of structured clinical-knowledge task. But the verification-burden dampener does not lift: the jagged-frontier evidence shows AI users trusting outputs outside a tool's genuine competence zone perform worse with misplaced confidence, and integrating pharmacology, comorbidity, and psychosocial factors into one safe plan for a specific patient is exactly the kind of judgment-heavy synthesis where that risk is highest. The program-level expectation for care-coordination content within accredited BSN curricula persists on its own slower clock. The rating stays Low: capability growth is real but the oversight requirement keeps pace with it.

A decade out, AI coordination-support tools will plausibly draft highly competent baseline care plans that a nurse edits and personalizes rather than generates from scratch, which is a meaningful shift in day-to-day workflow. Whether that constitutes eliminating the instrumental need to take this course is a harder call under wide capability uncertainty, but the verification-burden protection — a human must catch the plan that looks right and is wrong for this specific patient — is durable because error costs in disease management remain high and failures remain non-obvious. The rating holds Low rather than rising to Medium, reflecting that the course's core function is producing the oversight competence itself, not the plan-drafting task that AI increasingly performs on the nurse's behalf.
NUR 3770.d: This theory course builds on the student's previous knowledge of physiological and psychosocial components of illness. Magnet/Pathway's to Excellence concepts of Structural Empowerment and Exemplary Professional Practice and QSEN Competencies of Patient-Centered Care, Teamwork and Collaboration, and Evidence-Based Practice are integrated in the course to help clarify the role of the Care Coordinator of a baccalaureate-prepared nurse. Updates on genomics and genetics, pain management, the stress response, immune disorders, mental and behavioral health disorders, rehabilitative, and palliative, and end-of- life care are addressed. Nursing care coordination of acute and chronic disease concepts including pathophysiology, pharmacology, and physical assessment components are integrated with patient- centered, evidence-based disease management, and inter-professional collaboration to determine and provide safe, high quality, and cost- effective care.

r: This capstone-style course has students track evolving clinical trends and disseminate evidence across pathophysiology, pharmacology, and multiple specialty domains by accessing electronic information resources, with content shaped by each student's individual practice background. The core tasks — retrieving, synthesizing, and communicating current clinical evidence — map to getting-information and documenting activities that both task-exposure research and the enterprise-usage data flag as strongly exposed; this is close to the literature-synthesis work AI already performs well. Verification burden offers some protection: student-selected content spans direct patient-safety topics like error reduction, so a domain-competent reader still needs to check evidentiary claims. Because this course has no further required course depending on it in the sequence, its foundational-scaffolding protection is minimal. At 24 months the rating is Low, driven mainly by the residual verification dampener.

By 2031, AI research-synthesis tools will retrieve and summarize current clinical-practice trends across specialty domains with real facility, consistent with the fast capability-growth trend in structured knowledge-work tasks. The verification dampener loosens as tools mature and evidentiary summaries become easier to spot-check against source material, though it does not vanish entirely given the patient-safety topics students engage with. As a terminal, non-prerequisite course in the sequence, nothing about its foundational role holds the rating down further. The program-level expectation that BSN-completion students demonstrate this kind of evidence-tracking competence persists, but it is not tied to clinical clock hours. The rating rises to Medium: the execution tasks are substantially automatable and the remaining constraint is programmatic rather than protective at the task level.

A decade out, AI-driven clinical-evidence tracking and synthesis will likely be highly capable, and the instrumental case for a human performing the raw retrieval-and-summary tasks this course teaches weakens considerably. The institutional lock here is the program-level kind that can, plausibly, be revised over a ten-year window as accreditors and programs rethink how evidence-currency competence is assessed and delivered to already-licensed nurses returning for a completion degree rather than an initial license. The rating holds at Medium rather than advancing further because judging which trends and evidence generalize to a student's specific practice context retains a residual human-verification role, and because the capability trajectory, while fast, carries genuine uncertainty about how thoroughly AI substitutes for domain-situated clinical judgment by 2036.
NUR 3800.d: This course is designed to update students about evolving clinical issues and practice trends. Focus is on the role of the nurse in collecting and disseminating evidence to enhance evidence based practice. Core knowledge in pathophysiology, pharmacology, medical surgical nursing, pediatric nursing, obstetric nursing, psychiatric nursing, and community health nursing are explored. Specific course content reflects individual student nursing experiences and needs. Topics include patient safety and error reduction. The student is expected to access electronic information resources.

r: This course is a reflective, discussion-based examination of multicultural care, bias, and healthcare inequity, asking students to critically examine their own assumptions rather than perform any embodied or clinical task. The primary activity — reading, discussing, and writing critical self-reflection on bias and equity — maps to updating-and-using-relevant-knowledge and interpersonal-understanding categories that task-exposure research treats unevenly: the writing component is exposed, but genuine self-examination of bias is a critical-thinking, judgment-heavy process research associates with lower exposure. AI tools can already generate plausible-sounding reflections on bias and equity, which is itself a limitation — a generated reflection is not the same as a student's actual examined belief. Diversity, equity, and inclusion content of this kind remains a standard expectation in accredited nursing curricula. At 24 months the rating is Low.

By 2031, AI will readily produce polished essays on healthcare disparities, implicit bias, and cultural humility frameworks, and students will increasingly draft assignments with that assistance — a shift observed-usage data already anticipates given how dominant writing tasks are in current AI use. That erodes the writing-execution layer of the course substantially. It does not, however, substitute for the personal process of examining one's own biases, which is the course's stated pedagogical purpose and not reducible to producing correct-sounding text. GDPval-style evidence that top models still fall short of consistent expert-level performance on genuine deliverables reinforces that the authenticity gap matters here specifically. The rating rises to Medium: content generation is largely automatable, while the reflective competence the course targets is not equivalently substitutable.

A decade out, AI-generated reflection and bias-analysis writing will likely be difficult to distinguish from student work on the page, and the capability trajectory supports continued fast improvement in this kind of structured argumentative writing. Institutional expectations for cultural-competency and equity content in nursing curricula are durable but could plausibly be restructured over a ten-year window, loosening the program-level cap that currently holds the course at Medium rather than allowing it to rise to High. The genuine hedge is pedagogical rather than technical: whether the course still achieves its purpose once its written deliverables are AI-assistable is an open assessment-design question about how faculty verify authentic reflection, not a claim that the underlying human self-examination competence itself has become unnecessary.
NUR 3810.d: This course will provide nursing and pre-nursing students with the tools necessary to understand how multicultural care has been and is now being provided to patients and their families. It will bring to light the discrepancies and biases to people of color in the healthcare world and examine what we can do about it for more equity today. This course would help decrease stereotype threats by showing students diversity and have them examine their own biases.

r: The applied work is bedside critical-care nursing, built on the AACN's Essentials of Critical Care Orientation: hemodynamic assessment, ventilator and drip titration, skill-based simulation labs, and supervised clinical practice with acutely unstable patients. These tasks map to O*NET's physical-execution, monitoring-processes, and caring-for-others activities -- precisely the categories task-exposure research places outside AI's competitive frontier, and observed-usage data shows almost none of this real-time bedside work appearing in current AI use. Verification burden is extreme: a missed deterioration signal or incorrect titration is a life-threatening, non-obvious failure, so oversight must come from a human who holds the clinical knowledge itself. Selective admission and required skill-lab and clinical hours mean the course cannot be satisfied without supervised patient contact. At 24 months nothing in AI's observed trajectory substitutes for this embodied skill acquisition, so the instrumental need to take the course is fully intact.

By 2031, AI-based early-warning analytics, smart-monitor alerting, and documentation support will plausibly be more embedded in critical-care units, and the METR/Epoch capability-doubling trend suggests real gains in decision-support tools. That augments the bedside nurse; it does not perform hands-on hemodynamic assessment, line management, or the skill-lab competencies this course certifies. The jagged-frontier finding is relevant here -- outside AI's competence zone, reliance on AI outputs without expert verification produces materially worse accuracy, and critical-care judgment calls sit squarely outside that zone. Clinical-hour and skill-lab requirements tied to specialty practice standards do not relax on a five-year catalog cycle, and diffusion data shows AI adoption still uneven across firms and settings. The instrumental case for a student needing this course remains essentially unchanged; the plausible shift is nurses supervising more AI-assisted monitoring tools, not being replaced in the bedside role.

Under a central-case ten-year view, ambient clinical intelligence and monitoring automation will likely be considerably more capable, and Acemoglu-style macro estimates still describe only modest aggregate productivity effects even from broad AI diffusion. Even so, the embodied core this course builds -- physical assessment, procedural skill, and real-time judgment with unstable patients -- is not the kind of task current evidence shows AI substituting for; it is dominated by the manual and interpersonal activities task-exposure research consistently ranks as low-exposure. Specialty critical-care preparation continues to depend on supervised, hands-on skill acquisition that a curriculum cannot replace with simulation or AI tooling alone. The honest uncertainty concerns how much routine monitoring and documentation get automated around the nurse, not whether the underlying bedside competence remains necessary. The rating holds Low, though with a wider band than the 24-month horizon given the pace of capability growth.
NUR 3910.d: This course introduces the registered nurse to the field of critical care nursing. The American Association of Critical Care Nurses: "Essentials of Critical Care OrientationTM" is used as the basis for the course. Foundational knowledge, skill based labs and clinical practice provide basic critical care education to novice critical care nurses to provide safe patient care.

r: The applied work is emergency-department nursing built on ENA online orientation modules and Sheehy's Manual of Emergency Care: triage judgment, rapid physical assessment, skill-based laboratory practice, and supervised clinical practicums with acutely undifferentiated patients. These tasks map to O*NET's monitoring, caring-for-others, and rapid-decision-making activities, which task-exposure research consistently places among the least automatable, and observed-usage data shows negligible representation of real-time triage and bedside intervention in current AI use. Verification burden is severe: a missed red-flag finding in triage is a non-obvious, potentially fatal failure, so oversight must rest with a human who holds the emergency-nursing knowledge itself. Selective admission and required skill-lab and clinical-practicum hours mean the course cannot be completed without supervised patient contact. At 24 months the instrumental need to take this course is untouched by AI's current trajectory; embodiment and verification burden together keep the requirement fully intact.

By 2031, AI triage-support and decision-aid tools may be more common in emergency departments, consistent with the capability-doubling trend METR/Epoch describe, and such tools could plausibly speed documentation or flag deterioration risk. That is augmentation, not substitution: it does not perform physical assessment, wound care, or the rapid hands-on interventions the skill labs and practicums teach. The jagged-frontier research is directly relevant -- outside AI's competence zone, over-reliance on AI suggestions produces materially worse accuracy, and emergency triage judgment under uncertainty sits outside that zone. ENA-aligned curriculum and clinical-practicum requirements for emergency-nursing preparation do not relax within a five-year window, and diffusion data shows AI adoption remains uneven across healthcare settings. The instrumental case for the course stays essentially intact at five years; nurses will likely use more AI-assisted tools without those tools replacing the embodied competence being certified.

Over a ten-year horizon, monitoring and documentation automation in emergency care will likely be considerably more mature, but the central case still has emergency nurses personally performing triage assessment, physical intervention, and real-time judgment with unstable, high-acuity patients -- tasks defined by embodiment and interpersonal presence that task-exposure research treats as structurally low-exposure regardless of general capability gains. Acemoglu-style macro estimates suggest even broad AI diffusion produces only modest aggregate effects over a decade, reinforcing that transformation in high-stakes physical domains is slower than headline capability trends imply. Skill-lab and clinical-practicum requirements tied to emergency-specialty preparation are unlikely to be relaxed by a curriculum committee within this window. The genuine uncertainty is how much peripheral documentation and monitoring work shifts to AI tools around the nurse, not whether hands-on emergency competence remains something a student must acquire directly. The rating remains Low with appropriately wide bands.
NUR 3920.d: This course introduces the registered nurse to the essential principles of emergency nursing. The Emergency Nurses Association online orientation modules ™ and Sheehy's Manual of Emergency Care is used as the basis for the course. Foundational emergency nursing knowledge, skill-based laboratory, and clinical practicums provide basic education to novice emergency nurses to provide safe patient care.

r: The applied work here is population-level health promotion and disease-prevention analysis: community needs assessment, epidemiological reasoning about communicable disease and vulnerable populations, and enacting the leadership roles of advocate, change agent, collaborator, and teacher. Some of this -- literature review, drafting community health reports, synthesizing epidemiological data -- falls into Computer & Mathematical and writing-adjacent categories where observed-usage data shows AI already heavily used. But the advocacy, coalition-building, and teaching roles central to the course description are interpersonal and context-dependent, and task-exposure research finds critical-thinking-heavy work like this only partially exposed. Verification burden is moderate: population-health recommendations affect real communities and vulnerable groups, so an RN's judgment remains necessary to check AI-generated analysis. No explicit clinical or licensure mandate is stated in this description, so the institutional lock is contributory rather than absolute. At 24 months the course's tasks are only lightly touched by current AI capability.

By 2031, AI tools for epidemiological data synthesis, literature review, and community-report drafting will plausibly be routine, consistent with the capability-doubling trend and enterprise usage patterns skewed heavily toward automation. That could meaningfully compress the analytical and writing portions of this course's work. However, the leadership functions the description emphasizes -- advocate, change agent, collaborator, resource person, teacher working directly with communities and vulnerable populations -- remain interpersonal tasks where the jagged-frontier finding applies: AI performs worse and users calibrate trust poorly outside its competence zone, which includes context-sensitive community engagement. Verification burden keeps a credentialed nurse's judgment in the loop for population-health decisions with real consequences. Without an explicit clinical-hour or licensure mandate in this course's description, the institutional floor is weaker than for clinical courses, but it is not absent -- accreditation-aligned population-health content still anchors curricular structure. The instrumental case softens moderately but does not collapse.

Ten years out, AI-assisted population-health analytics could plausibly handle a substantial share of the data synthesis, epidemiological modeling, and report-generation tasks this course teaches, especially if adoption diffuses beyond the roughly 18% of firms using AI as of late 2025. But the course's leadership dimension -- earning community trust, mobilizing collaborators, teaching diverse populations, navigating cultural and ethical context -- depends on real-time interpersonal judgment that current evidence does not show AI performing reliably, and Acemoglu-style estimates suggest even broad diffusion yields only modest aggregate transformation over a decade. The rating is genuinely uncertain here: if population-health practice becomes primarily desk-based analytics work, exposure could rise toward Medium; if the advocacy and community-engagement core stays dominant, Low persists. Given the absence of an explicit clinical-hour lock in this description, this course carries somewhat less institutional protection than clinical practicum courses, warranting a wider hedge at ten years.
NUR 4000.d: This course provides the tools for critical analysis of the principles of health promotion and disease prevention of families, groups, and communities. Cultural diversity, ethics, legal, and political responsibility of the nurse is discussed. The leadership roles of advocate, change agent, collaborator, resource person, and teacher are emphasized. The learner applies theories and models from the fields of public health, education, and nursing, to community health nursing. Focus is placed on community needs assessment, epidemiology, communicable disease, vulnerable populations, and health risks across lifespan.

At 24 months the theoretical content is only lightly displaced.

By 2031, AI-assisted epidemiological synthesis and health-promotion literature review will plausibly be routine study and practice tools, in line with the capability-doubling trend and heavy enterprise-API usage in analytical tasks. Over ten years, AI tools could plausibly absorb a considerable share of the epidemiological-analysis and theory-synthesis work this course covers, particularly as adoption diffuses further; but Acemoglu-style macro estimates still project only modest aggregate transformation even under broad uptake. The leadership and advocacy core -- teaching, mobilizing collaborators, applying ethical and cultural judgment across populations -- is not shown by current evidence to be reliably AI-performed, keeping a meaningful non-automatable center to the course. The genuine uncertainty is whether population-health theory instruction increasingly relies on AI-assisted analysis while the advocacy competencies stay human-anchored, or whether the whole domain becomes more augmented than instrumental. The rating stays Low, with a wider hedge reflecting that uncertainty at the ten-year mark.
NUR 4010.d: Students in this course gain the tools to critically analyze the principles of health promotion and disease prevention in families, groups, communities, and, populations. Cultural diversity, ethics, legal and political responsibility of the nurse are discussed. The leadership roles of advocate, change agent, collaborator, resource person, and the teacher are emphasized. The learner applies theories and models from the fields of public health, education, and nursing to community health nursing. Focus is placed on epidemiology, communicable disease, and health risks across the lifespan.

r: The applied work is the practical clinical fieldwork required for population and community health nursing: applying public-health and nursing theory in real community settings, conducting community assessment, and using QSEN and Magnet/AAACN nurse-sensitive-indicator frameworks to evaluate the quality of community-based care. This is embodied practicum work -- direct engagement with communities, agencies, and individuals in real time -- mapping to O*NET's caring-for-others and interpersonal-relationship activities that task-exposure research places among the least automatable categories. Verification burden is high: community-health field decisions affect real populations and require a licensed RN's judgment, and enrollment itself requires a verified active RN license. No AI system performs the supervised field placement a practicum credits. At 24 months the course's instrumental necessity is fully intact -- it is defined by the requirement that a real, licensed nurse complete real clinical hours in the community, which current AI capability cannot substitute.

By 2031, AI tools may help with community-assessment data aggregation or documentation that supports practicum work, consistent with growing enterprise use of AI for analytical and writing tasks. That does not touch the practicum's defining feature: a licensed nurse physically completing supervised community-health clinical hours, applying QSEN and nurse-sensitive-indicator standards in real encounters. The jagged-frontier finding underscores why this matters -- field judgment in unpredictable community settings sits outside AI's reliable competence zone, and mis-calibrated trust in AI outputs there could produce real harm. Program requirements verifying active RN licensure before enrollment and crediting the clinical-hour component are not the kind of structure a five-year catalog cycle relaxes. The instrumental case for taking this practicum remains essentially unchanged; any AI role would be peripheral documentation support around a clinical-hour requirement that is, by design, not simulatable.

Even under a ten-year horizon with substantially more capable AI decision-support and monitoring tools, the central case still requires a licensed nurse to complete supervised, hands-on community-health clinical hours -- the practicum's entire instrumental purpose. Embodiment and real-time interpersonal engagement with community members and agencies keep this work in the task-exposure categories research consistently finds least automatable, and Acemoglu-style estimates suggest broad AI diffusion produces only modest aggregate change over a decade, well short of displacing supervised clinical training structures. The plausible shift is that AI tools increasingly support the documentation and data-aggregation work around the practicum, not that the clinical-hour requirement itself is removed. Some uncertainty exists around how community-health delivery models might evolve with AI-assisted public-health tools, but the requirement that a student personally complete verified clinical hours is unlikely to erode. The rating holds Low with high confidence given the explicit licensure and clinical-hour anchor.
NUR 4020.d: The focus of this course is to provide the practical clinical experience required for Population and Community Health Nursing. The learner applies theory from fields of public health, education, and nursing to population and community health nursing. Focus is placed on community assessment, QSEN, Magnet Status, and the American Association of Ambulatory Care Nurses - Nurse Sensitive Indicators to consider how to achieve quality care in the community.

r: The applied work is introductory nursing informatics: navigating an EHR to identify essential documentation elements, analyzing EHR-derived data against literature and national benchmarks, reviewing patient-satisfaction survey data, and applying ethical, legal, and regulatory data-privacy standards. This is squarely within Computer & Mathematical and data-analysis activities, the category observed-usage data identifies as AI's largest current-use domain, so introductory-level EHR navigation and benchmark comparison are already assisted by existing tools. Verification burden is moderate, not minimal: interpreting clinical data validity and applying privacy and regulatory judgment still needs a nurse who understands both the clinical context and the compliance framework, so AI outputs require expert review. No explicit clinical or licensure hours are described, and this content contributes to but does not singlehandedly satisfy accreditation informatics expectations. At 24 months, foundational informatics literacy is still best learned directly, so the course's instrumental need remains Low but visibly more contestable than clinical courses.

By 2031, AI-assisted EHR analytics, automated benchmarking against national quality indicators, and natural-language summarization of patient-satisfaction data will plausibly be standard tools in clinical informatics, consistent with the steep capability-doubling trend and heavy enterprise-API use in analytical tasks. Much of what this introductory course teaches -- manually locating and comparing EHR data elements against literature and benchmarks -- increasingly resembles a task AI performs competently, shifting the rating toward Medium. Verification burden still matters: privacy, regulatory compliance, and clinically meaningful interpretation of flagged data patterns require a human who understands both nursing practice and the informatics tooling, which tempers full erosion. As a prerequisite feeding into leadership coursework and the capstone, the course retains some scaffolding role. The instrumental case weakens meaningfully at five years as AI absorbs more of the data-navigation and benchmarking work, though the compliance-literacy and clinical-interpretation core still argues for a student learning this directly.

Ten years out, informatics tooling embedded directly in EHR platforms will likely automate much of the routine data-comparison and benchmarking work this course introduces, and despite Acemoglu-style estimates of modest aggregate productivity effects, informatics is one of the more digitally native corners of nursing curricula and plausibly among the faster-diffusing. Genuine uncertainty remains about whether nurses will still need to personally execute EHR navigation and benchmark analysis, or whether their informatics role shifts entirely toward interpreting and governing AI-generated analytics -- a different but still real skill this introductory course partly builds. Regulatory, privacy, and compliance judgment is likely to stay human-anchored longer than the data-manipulation tasks themselves, keeping some instrumental core intact. Given the course's prerequisite role toward leadership and capstone work, complete erosion is unlikely even in an aggressive capability scenario. The rating holds at Medium, reflecting real but partial and still-uncertain exposure rather than displacement.
NUR 4040.d: This course introduces the student to the process of collecting and analyzing data used to improve the quality of care patients receive and enhance their safety. Course content aligns with Magnet/Pathways to Excellence of Empirical Outcomes, New Knowledge, Innovations, and Improvement and QSEN Competencies of Evidence-Based Practice (EBP), Quality Improvement, Safety and Informatics. A basic overview of nursing informatics and how it applies to clinical practice will be explored. During this course students will navigate an electronic health record (EHR) to identify essential information that must be available in a common database that documents patient care. Analysis of data from the EHR will compared with current relevant literature, and selected national benchmarking goals. Introduction to patient satisfaction survey scores will be examined as they relate to patient-centered care, quality and safety to improve overall practice. Ethical, legal, and regulatory considerations are upheld related to data security, confidentiality, and patient's right to privacy.

r: The applied work is analyzing ethical theories, principles, and decision-making models and applying them to concrete professional-practice dilemmas through case discussion and critical reasoning about codes of ethics. This is discussion- and writing-based content, overlapping with generalist argumentation tasks where observed-usage data shows meaningful current AI use, but task-exposure research also finds that science- and critical-thinking-heavy work is negatively associated with exposure, and applied ethical judgment in live nursing dilemmas leans toward that protective end. Verification burden is real: nursing ethics dilemmas carry professional and patient-welfare consequences, and an AI-generated ethical analysis needs a practitioner's judgment to validate against actual clinical context, so oversight cannot be waived. No explicit clinical hours or licensure gate applies to this seminar-style course; its institutional weight comes from standard accreditation curricular expectations rather than a course-specific mandate. At 24 months, structured ethical reasoning instruction remains something a student needs to do directly.

By 2031, AI tools capable of generating plausible ethical analyses, summarizing case precedents, and drafting decision frameworks will likely be more common study aids, consistent with the capability-doubling trend and strong enterprise use of AI for writing and reasoning-adjacent tasks. That could ease some of the drafting and case-summary work in this course. However, the jagged-frontier research is instructive: AI performance degrades and user trust becomes poorly calibrated once problems move outside its competence zone, and unscripted ethical dilemmas involving real patients, families, and institutional pressures are exactly this kind of ambiguous, high-stakes territory. Verification burden stays elevated because a wrong ethical framing in practice has professional and human consequences. Accreditation-driven curricular expectations for ethics content persist across a five-year cycle even without a course-specific licensure mandate. The instrumental case for structured ethics instruction remains largely intact, tempered only modestly by better AI-assisted case preparation.

A decade out, AI systems will likely produce increasingly sophisticated ethical analyses and decision-support frameworks, and it is plausible that some case-discussion preparation shifts toward AI-assisted tools. Even so, task-exposure research's consistent finding that critical-thinking-intensive work resists exposure, combined with the genuinely adversarial and context-dependent nature of real ethical dilemmas in nursing practice, argues against assuming this course's core function is substitutable. Acemoglu-style macro projections of modest aggregate change over a decade reinforce that transformation in judgment-heavy professional education is likely to be gradual rather than displacing. The wide uncertainty here concerns how much of ethics education becomes AI-assisted case analysis versus how much remains live discussion and applied reasoning under supervision; both are plausible, and the balance is not confidently predictable this far out. The rating holds Low, with the explicit caveat that this is among the more contestable Low ratings in the batch.
NUR 4150.d: This course prepares the professional nursing student to analyze ethical issues that emerge in the practice of nursing. This course introduces the student to ethical theories and principles as well as ethical decision making models applied to professional nursing. Students apply critical thinking concepts to applicable codes of ethics, ethical theories, principles, and rules in discussing the ethical dilemmas encountered in professional practice. Values and beliefs are examined in the context of ethical issues, role development, and application in health care.

r: The applied work is nursing leadership and management theory: organizational theory, health-policy and regulatory frameworks, evidence-based-practice application, and business economics as they apply to managing nursing units and practice environments. This content closely resembles general management coursework -- analyzing organizational structures, policy documents, and economic frameworks -- squarely within the Computer & Mathematical and writing-adjacent categories observed-usage data identifies as AI's largest current-use domain, and Copilot-style productivity gains show large speedups on structured analytical and drafting tasks. Verification burden is moderate rather than low: management and policy analysis benefits from expert review but errors are not immediately safety-critical the way bedside care is, so the dampening effect is limited. No clinical hours or licensure gate apply; the institutional anchor is standard accreditation curricular content rather than a course-specific mandate. At 24 months, AI already meaningfully assists the drafting and analytical work central to this course, supporting a Medium rating.

By 2031, AI tools for organizational analysis, policy synthesis, staffing-economics modeling, and management-report drafting will plausibly be well-embedded in both nursing-leadership coursework and practice, consistent with the steep capability-doubling trend, professional-writing productivity studies showing large time savings alongside quality gains, and heavy enterprise-API use for exactly these analytical and writing categories. The course's content -- theory, policy, and economics applied through case analysis and written work -- maps closely onto tasks AI already performs competently, and diffusion pressure in healthcare administration is likely to accelerate over five years even from today's uneven adoption baseline. Verification burden remains real but not severe enough to offset the shift, since most of the graded work here is analytical and written rather than real-time clinical judgment. Institutional lock is weak -- no licensure or clinical-hour mandate anchors this course. The instrumental case for a student needing to do this analytical work unaided weakens substantially by five years.

Over a ten-year horizon, it is plausible that AI systems handle the great majority of routine organizational analysis, regulatory-compliance review, and management-report generation this course trains toward, especially if healthcare administration follows the broader diffusion trend beyond today's roughly 18%-of-firms baseline. The course's task profile -- applying leadership and management theory through written analysis rather than embodied or real-time interpersonal action -- lacks the embodiment or extreme verification burden that protects clinical courses in this catalog. Acemoglu-style estimates of modest aggregate productivity effects introduce some caution against overconfidence, and genuine leadership skills like team motivation and interpersonal influence retain a human core that is harder to specify. But the analytical and written management-theory content that dominates this course's description is well inside AI's demonstrated strengths. The rating is High with an appropriate hedge: the interpersonal leadership dimension is more resistant than the analytical coursework, and that gap is the main source of uncertainty.
NUR 4300.d: The student in this course will develop as a professional nurse by investigating leadership and management theories and principles. This course emphasizes management, leadership, organizational theories, policy, regulatory requirements, evidence- based practice, and business economics.

r: The applied work is a reflective synthesis: narrating the student's program journey, linking theoretical constructs from prior coursework -- evidence-based-practice research, informatics, leadership -- to Magnet concepts, and summarizing how those concepts and QSEN goals relate to improved patient outcomes. This is fundamentally a professional-writing and synthesis task -- connecting previously covered material into a coherent narrative -- which productivity research on professional writing finds AI already accelerates substantially, and which observed-usage data places within the largest current AI-use categories. Verification burden is moderate rather than low: an instructor still needs to confirm the synthesis accurately reflects the student's own learning and program-specific framework, but errors here are not safety-critical in the way clinical judgment is. No licensure or clinical-hour mandate applies to this capstone; institutional weight comes only from generic program-completion structure. At 24 months, AI can already meaningfully draft and structure this kind of reflective synthesis, supporting a Medium rating.

By 2031, AI-assisted synthesis and reflective writing will plausibly be routine, consistent with professional-writing productivity research showing large time savings with quality gains and with the steep capability-doubling trend in what AI can competently produce. A capstone assignment built around connecting previously learned theoretical constructs into a coherent narrative account is close to a canonical high-exposure writing task; task-exposure research consistently finds writing and synthesis positively associated with AI exposure. The primary check against full automation is academic-integrity verification -- confirming the reflection represents genuine student learning -- which is an institutional-policy concern rather than a task-capability constraint, and does not function as a strong lock in the sense used elsewhere in this framework. No accreditation or licensure requirement anchors this specific reflective-paper format. The instrumental case for a student personally performing this synthesis work, absent integrity safeguards, weakens substantially by five years.

A decade out, AI systems will very plausibly be capable of producing polished, contextually appropriate reflective syntheses linking coursework to professional frameworks with minimal human drafting, and nothing in this course's description -- no clinical hours, no licensure gate, no embodied task -- provides institutional protection against that trend. The genuine constraint is pedagogical and administrative rather than technical: programs may redesign capstone assessment specifically because the current narrative-synthesis format becomes trivially producible by AI, which is itself evidence of high exposure rather than a counterargument. Acemoglu-style macro estimates of modest economy-wide effects are a weaker consideration for a single writing-intensive assessment than for embodied clinical work. The wide-uncertainty caveat here is less about capability, which is already strong for this task type, and more about how assessment design responds. The rating remains High, reflecting that the instrumental task as currently described is highly automatable rather than protected by any binding constraint.
NUR 4860.d: This course provides nursing students with the opportunity to narrate their journey of Magnet® learning throughout the program. In this course, students will describe the process of effective change by linking theoretical constructs and philosophical tenets of previous classes in the program. Most notably, previous work from the Evidence Based Practice Using Nursing Research (NUR 3400), Quality & Patient Safety Using Nursing Informatics (NUR 4040), and Leadership and Management in Professional Nursing Practice (NUR 4300) will be synthesized to illustrate how Magnet® concepts were used to inform care and improve patient outcomes. An important objective of this class is for the student to summarize the relationship in their own practice between the Magnet® concepts and QSEN goals for improved patient outcomes.
